tutorials.title: 1. OpenCV fundamentals for IoT visual sensors
tutorials.summary: Represent images as arrays, convert color, threshold pixels and publish a useful measurement.

lessons.title: Pixels, channels and memory
lessons.text: An image is an array with height, width and channels. The browser supplies RGBA bytes: red, green, blue and alpha, each from 0 to 255. Python OpenCV normally loads files in BGR order, so the conversion flag must match the source. These labs create 128 × 128 synthetic scenes and process them with actual local OpenCV. A microcontroller can consume the resulting event even when a more capable companion computer performs the image processing.

lessons.title: Turn intensity into a mask
lessons.text: Grayscale conversion combines color channels into one intensity value. A binary threshold selects a pixel when its grayscale value exceeds T. The white pixels in the output are the selected set, not a confidence score. Change scene brightness while holding T constant: a lamp can disappear from the mask without physically moving. Gaussian smoothing can suppress small variations but also softens boundaries. Always inspect the source and processed images together.

lessons.title: Reduce a mask to a device message
lessons.text: Count selected pixels and divide by the total image area to obtain a fraction. The IoT preview reports a detected event when at least 16 pixels are selected. This is a deliberately simple rule: a bright reflection could also trigger it. Open the integration bench, start its virtual ESP32 and send the observation. The browser calls the virtual /on or /off HTTP route and displays the actual response. Pixel processing and device transport are separate stages.

formulas.title: Grayscale intensity
formulas.symbols: R, G, B: 8-bit channel values; Y: approximate grayscale intensity. This is a conventional image conversion, not calibrated optical power.
formulas.example: For R = 100, G = 150, B = 200, Y ≈ 140.75, rounded to an 8-bit value.

formulas.title: Binary selection and area fraction
formulas.equation: M(x,y) = 1 if Y(x,y) > T else 0;  f = ΣM / (WH)
formulas.symbols: T: intensity threshold; M: binary selection; W, H: image dimensions (pixels); f: dimensionless selected fraction.

steps: Inspect the default IoT scene and threshold mask. Record selected pixels and centroid.
Lower brightness to 0.4 at threshold 150. Explain why the visual event disappears.
Lower the threshold until the target returns, then observe when background pixels are also selected.
Connect the integration bench, start devices and send both a detected and a no-target observation. Compare HTTP /on and /off responses.

practice.prompt: How many pixels are in a 128 × 128 image?
practice.explanation: Multiply width by height. Channels affect byte count, not the number of pixels.

practice.prompt: Which source channel order does browser ImageData use?
practice.explanation: ImageData stores red, green, blue and alpha; Python cv2.imread normally returns BGR.

questions.prompt: For a binary threshold of 150, grayscale intensity 150 is…
questions.explanation: THRESH_BINARY selects values strictly greater than the threshold.

questions.prompt: 512 selected pixels in a 128 × 128 image occupy…
questions.explanation: 512/16384 = 0.03125; multiply by 100 to express percent.

questions.prompt: What can a darker scene do with a fixed threshold?

options.text: Make a real target disappear from the mask

questions.explanation: A threshold responds to measured intensity; lighting affects that measurement.

questions.prompt: Must an ESP32 run the entire vision pipeline to receive an event?

options.text: Only if it has a propeller
No; a companion can process images and send a bounded event
Yes; image processing and transport are identical

questions.explanation: Separate perception from device control through a defined message interface.

questions.prompt: Does a white mask pixel mean the detector is 100% confident?

options.text: No, it only passed the pixel rule

questions.explanation: A binary mask encodes selection rather than calibrated confidence.

tutorials.title: 2. OpenCV color segmentation for drone alignment
tutorials.summary: Find a landing-marker color, calculate an image offset and translate it into a device signal.

lessons.title: Choose a color space for the task
lessons.text: HSV separates hue, saturation and value. OpenCV uses hue 0–179 for an 8-bit HSV image, while saturation and value use 0–255. The sandbox selects hue 40–90, saturation at least 80 and value at least 60 to find the green pad. Its white H decoration is intentionally excluded. Color segmentation does not recognize an H or prove the surface is suitable for landing; it selects pixels matching a configured color range.

lessons.title: Find the center of selected pixels
lessons.text: The centroid is the average x and y of selected pixels. Image x increases rightward and image y downward. Normalize horizontal displacement by half the image width to express a scale-independent offset near −1 to 1. Move the pad with the offset slider and inspect the sign. If the mask is empty, the centroid is undefined: produce a no-target observation instead of inventing a center coordinate.

lessons.title: Separate visual alignment from flight control
lessons.text: A camera offset is not directly a motor command. A deployed drone needs camera calibration, camera-to-body transforms, target validation and a flight controller that handles attitude and failsafe behavior. This lab exposes a normalized offset and an aligned flag. The integration bench maps left, center and right observations to 1150, 1200 and 1250 µs on one clamped, props-off ESC. That demonstrates an interface, not an autonomous landing controller.

formulas.title: Mask centroid
formulas.equation: cx = Σ(xM) / ΣM;  cy = Σ(yM) / ΣM
formulas.symbols: M: binary mask; x, y: pixel coordinates; cx, cy: centroid in pixels. Defined only when ΣM > 0.
formulas.example: Two selected pixels at x = 20 and x = 40 give cx = 30 px.

formulas.title: Normalized horizontal offset
formulas.symbols: cx: horizontal centroid (px); W: image width (px); ex: dimensionless signed offset. Camera orientation must be handled before using it on hardware.

steps: Keep HSV mode and move the landing marker to offset +25 px. Inspect positive horizontal error.
Narrow the hue interval so green is excluded; verify no target and an undefined centroid.
Restore hue 40–90, add occlusion and compare centroid shift with the visible target.
Start connected devices and send left, center and right observations. Inspect the actual props-off ESC pulse changes.

practice.prompt: What hue range does OpenCV use for 8-bit HSV?
practice.explanation: The 8-bit OpenCV hue representation uses half-degree scaling across 0–179.

practice.prompt: Why is the white H missing from the green mask?

options.text: It has too little saturation for this selection

practice.explanation: The mask requires saturation at least 80; nearly white pixels have low saturation.

questions.prompt: Selected x coordinates 10, 20 and 30 have centroid…
questions.explanation: Add coordinates and divide by the count: 60/3 = 20.

questions.prompt: What should an empty mask produce?
questions.explanation: Division by zero cannot produce a meaningful centroid.

questions.prompt: A marker to the right of the image center has…

options.text: Negative error in every camera convention

questions.explanation: This image convention assigns increasing x to the right.

questions.prompt: What does the props-off ESC integration demonstrate?

options.text: Mapping a perception result into a bounded device signal

questions.explanation: The clamped motor experiment tests a signal adapter without implementing flight navigation.

questions.prompt: Which is required before using image offsets on a real drone?

options.text: Camera calibration and camera-to-body coordinate handling
Treating every green object as safe ground

questions.explanation: Image coordinates must be related to the vehicle and the target validated.

tutorials.title: 3. OpenCV edges and ROS 2 robot integration
tutorials.summary: Extract a line boundary, compute steering and publish a Twist with a clear coordinate convention.

lessons.title: Edges describe intensity changes
lessons.text: An edge is a local intensity transition. Canny uses image derivatives, suppresses broad responses and links weaker edges to stronger ones through hysteresis thresholds. The sandbox first applies optional Gaussian blur, then calls cv.Canny with a 3 × 3 derivative aperture and L2 gradient magnitude. The output outlines the white line instead of filling its interior. A boundary map is not a semantic label: floor texture and shadows can also create edges.

lessons.title: Convert image error into a steering request
lessons.text: The line centroid provides a simple horizontal error. In this lab, a line to the right requests negative robot yaw because positive ROS yaw is counterclockwise. The adapter uses angular.z = −ex rad/s and a fixed forward request of 0.15 m/s when a target exists. With no selected target it requests zero velocity. This rule assumes an upright forward-facing camera and a simple scene; the browser does not simulate perspective calibration or a real camera mount.

lessons.title: Publish perception results through a ROS 2 node
lessons.text: A real integration reads frames, validates detection, creates a geometry_msgs/msg/Twist and publishes it on the driver topic. The accompanying Python example shows a ROS 2 timer node reading a saved test frame, with camera acquisition left as a separate deployment step. Match the subscription name and units. Configure a driver timeout independently of the publisher: a crashed perception node must not leave a stale velocity request active indefinitely.

formulas.title: Image gradient magnitude
formulas.equation: G = √(Gx² + Gy²)
formulas.symbols: Gx, Gy: horizontal and vertical image derivatives in intensity units per pixel; G: gradient magnitude. Canny also includes suppression and hysteresis.
formulas.example: For Gx = 3 and Gy = 4, G = 5 intensity units per pixel.

formulas.title: Image-based yaw request
formulas.equation: ωcmd = −K ex
formulas.symbols: ωcmd: yaw rate (rad/s); ex: normalized horizontal image error; K: gain in rad/s per unit error, 1 in this adapter. Assumes an upright forward camera.
formulas.example: For ex = +0.25 and K = 1, request angular.z = −0.25 rad/s, a clockwise turn.

steps: Compare the source line with the Canny edge map; identify its two boundaries.
Move the line right and verify negative angular.z in the message preview.
Compare no blur with a 5 × 5 Gaussian kernel after increasing pixel noise.
Start the integration bench and send the observation. Compare robot yaw before and after the one-second motion interval.

practice.prompt: Gx = 3 and Gy = 4 produce which L2 gradient magnitude?
practice.explanation: The magnitude is √(3²+4²) = 5.

practice.prompt: Does a Canny edge map fill the whole object?

options.text: Yes, every interior pixel is selected
It only produces a class name

practice.explanation: Edges represent intensity changes around boundaries.

questions.prompt: A line at ex = +0.25 produces which yaw request here?
questions.explanation: The adapter applies ωcmd = −ex rad/s for its camera convention.

questions.prompt: Which message carries the robot velocity command?
questions.explanation: Twist carries linear and angular velocity components.

questions.prompt: Why add Gaussian blur before edge detection?

options.text: To reduce small image variations before differentiation

questions.explanation: Differentiation is sensitive to noise; smoothing trades detail for reduced variation.

questions.prompt: What should this adapter send when no target is found?
questions.explanation: No-target behavior should be explicit; this teaching adapter requests stop.

questions.prompt: Where should the stale-command timeout be enforced?

options.text: In the receiving driver/controller, independently of perception
It is automatic for every ROS topic

questions.explanation: A receiver must handle missing updates even if the publisher has crashed.

tutorials.title: 4. OpenCV morphology: clean up a noisy mask
tutorials.summary: Remove salt-and-pepper specks from a threshold mask with erosion, dilation, opening and closing, then measure what changed.

lessons.title: Erosion and dilation with a kernel
lessons.text: Morphology edits a binary mask with a small shape: the structuring element, or kernel. This lab uses a square kernel of 3 × 3, 5 × 5 or 7 × 7 pixels. Erosion keeps a white pixel only when every pixel under the kernel is white: shapes shrink and smaller specks vanish. Dilation turns a pixel white when any pixel under the kernel is white: shapes grow and small gaps close. The speckled preset mask has 1158 pixels. A 3 × 3 erosion leaves 279; a 3 × 3 dilation spreads to 5564.

lessons.title: Opening removes specks; closing fills holes
lessons.text: Opening is an erosion followed by a dilation with the same kernel. The erosion deletes specks too small to hold the kernel; the dilation regrows the shapes that survive. Closing runs the other way. It fills small dark holes and gaps but keeps isolated white specks. The preset thresholds the lamp scene, with 8% salt-and-pepper specks, at 150. The plain mask has 537 connected components and IoU 0.416. A 3 × 3 opening leaves 1 component and IoU 0.878; a 3 × 3 closing leaves 416 components.

lessons.title: Read the counts and choose a kernel
lessons.text: The lab counts pixels and connected components before and after the operation. A component is a group of white pixels joined through any of their 8 neighbours. After the 3 × 3 opening, all 454 selected pixels lie inside the 517-pixel lamp. The 63 it misses are 25 dark specks and pixels trimmed around them: opening cannot fill holes. Larger kernels cut the lamp: 5 × 5 splits it in 2 with IoU 0.716, and 7 × 7 gives 0.294. Real specks change every frame; these generated ones do not.

formulas.title: Erosion and dilation
formulas.equation: erode(x,y) = min M(x+i, y+j);  dilate(x,y) = max M(x+i, y+j),  for (i, j) in B
formulas.symbols: M: binary mask with values 0 or 255; B: the k × k kernel centred on the pixel; i, j: offsets inside B (px). On a binary mask, min means "all white" and max means "any white".
formulas.example: A lone white pixel with a 3 × 3 kernel: erosion removes it, because its neighbours are black. Dilation grows it into a 3 × 3 block of 9 pixels.

formulas.title: Opening, closing and iterations
formulas.equation: open(M) = dilate(erode(M));  close(M) = erode(dilate(M))
formulas.symbols: Both steps use the same kernel B. With n iterations, an opening erodes n times and then dilates n times. For square kernels, two 3 × 3 passes reach as far as one 5 × 5 pass.
formulas.example: Preset: a 3 × 3 opening turns 1158 pixels in 537 components into 454 pixels in 1 component, and IoU rises from 0.416 to 0.878.

steps: Open the preset. Record pixels and connected components before and after the 3 × 3 opening, and the IoU.
Change the operation to close. Explain why the specks survive and more than 400 components remain.
Try erode, then dilate. Compare each selected-pixel count with the opened mask and explain how the lamp changes size.
Return to open and raise the kernel to 5 × 5, then 7 × 7. Record IoU each time, and compare the IoT bright_fraction with the clean lamp value of 0.0316.

practice.prompt: A lone white pixel meets a 3 × 3 erosion. What happens to it?

options.text: It stays, because erosion only changes large shapes

practice.explanation: Erosion keeps a pixel only when the whole kernel covers white pixels. A lone pixel has black neighbours.

practice.prompt: Which operation removes isolated white specks but keeps larger shapes?
practice.explanation: Opening erodes the specks away, then dilates the surviving shapes back toward their size.

questions.prompt: Why does closing alone fail to clean the speckled preset?

options.text: Closing fills dark holes and gaps, so isolated white specks survive

questions.explanation: Dilation grows each white speck and erosion shrinks it back. 416 components remain after a 3 × 3 closing.

questions.prompt: Which 3 × 3 operation grew the speckled mask from 1158 to 5564 pixels?
questions.explanation: Dilation turns a pixel white when any pixel under the kernel is white, so every speck grows.

questions.prompt: After the 3 × 3 opening, IoU is 0.878, not 1. Why?

options.text: Dark specks inside the lamp leave holes that opening cannot fill

questions.explanation: All 454 selected pixels lie inside the 517-pixel lamp. The 63 missing pixels sit at and around its dark specks.

questions.prompt: What did raising the opening kernel from 3 × 3 to 7 × 7 do here?

options.text: It trimmed the lamp itself, and IoU fell to 0.294

questions.explanation: Opening removes every region that cannot hold the kernel, including lamp pixels near its dark specks.

questions.prompt: Before the opening, the mask has 537 connected components. What does that mean?

options.text: There are 537 separate white groups: the lamp and 536 specks

questions.explanation: Components count groups of touching white pixels. Here the specks hold 1 to 5 pixels each.

tutorials.title: 5. OpenCV contours and shape analysis
tutorials.summary: Trace object outlines, measure area, perimeter and circularity, and label simple shapes from their polygon corners.

lessons.title: From a mask to outlines
lessons.text: findContours follows the border of each white region in a binary mask and returns the outline as a list of points. The lab first thresholds the shapes scene at 128. It asks for external outlines only, so holes inside a region are ignored. CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE keeps only the end points of straight runs. Every white region gets an outline, including specks: with 5% specks and a minimum area of 0, the lab lists 340 contours. A minimum area of 50 px² drops the specks and keeps the three shapes, sorted left to right.

lessons.title: Area, perimeter and circularity
lessons.text: contourArea returns the area enclosed by the outline polygon, and arcLength returns its length. Both follow the centres of the border pixels, so the 25 × 25-pixel square reports area 576 (24 × 24) and perimeter 96. Circularity 4πA/P² is 1 for a perfect circle and π/4 ≈ 0.785 for any square. The pixel circle scores 0.859 and the triangle 0.523. The output outlines each kept shape in red with a blue bounding box. The mask fills them, so IoU is 1. The IoT preview sends only detection and area, never labels.

lessons.title: Approximate polygons and label shapes
lessons.text: approxPolyDP simplifies an outline so that no original point lies farther than ε × perimeter from the new polygon. At ε = 0.04 even the circle drops to 4 corners, so the lab tests roundness before the four-corner rule. Three corners mean triangle; circularity of 0.83 or more means circle; 4 corners with width/height between 0.9 and 1.1 mean square. Specks roughen outlines: at 5% the circle scores 0.751 and becomes a polygon. Clean the mask first: in the companion script, a 3 × 3 closing then opening restores 0.873. These are hand-written rules, not a trained classifier.

formulas.title: Circularity
formulas.equation: C = 4πA / P²
formulas.symbols: A: area enclosed by the outline (px²); P: perimeter (px); C: dimensionless, 1 for a perfect circle and π/4 ≈ 0.785 for any square. A pixelated circle scores below 1: 0.859 here.
formulas.example: The lab square has A = 576 px² and P = 96 px, so C = 4π × 576 / 96² ≈ 0.785.

formulas.title: Polygon tolerance and aspect ratio
formulas.equation: dmax = ε × P;  aspect = w / h
formulas.symbols: ε: lab setting, a fraction of the perimeter; P: perimeter (px); dmax: largest distance (px) allowed between the outline and its simplified polygon; w, h: bounding-box width and height (px).
formulas.example: The circle perimeter is 77.3 px. At ε = 0.04, dmax ≈ 3.1 px and 4 corners remain. At ε = 0.01, dmax ≈ 0.77 px and 12 corners remain.

steps: Open the preset. Read each shape's label, area, perimeter, corner count and circularity, and confirm IoU 1.
Lower ε to 0.01. Count the circle's corners and explain why its label stays circle.
Set specks to 5% and the minimum area to 0. Count the contours, then raise the minimum area to 50 and compare the circle's circularity and label.
Remove the specks and raise the minimum area to 450. Explain which shape disappears and why.

practice.prompt: What circularity does any perfect square have?
practice.explanation: For side s: 4π s² / (4s)² = π/4.

practice.prompt: With 5% specks and minimum area 0, why does the lab list 340 contours?

options.text: Every white speck gets its own outline
Each shape is split into 100 parts

practice.explanation: findContours outlines every white region. The minimum-area filter is what removes the specks.

questions.prompt: The 25 × 25-pixel square reports area 576. Why not 625?

options.text: The outline runs through border-pixel centres, enclosing 24 × 24

questions.explanation: Contour points sit at pixel centres, so the enclosed polygon is one pixel narrower in each direction.

questions.prompt: At ε = 0.04 the circle simplifies to 4 corners. Why is it still labelled circle?

options.text: The lab checks circularity ≥ 0.83 before the four-corner rule
Its bounding box is not square

questions.explanation: The circle's circularity is 0.859, so the roundness rule wins before the 4-corner rule.

questions.prompt: Raising ε from 0.01 to 0.04 gives the circle's polygon…
questions.explanation: A larger tolerance lets the polygon skip more outline points.

questions.prompt: What does the minimum-area setting do?

options.text: Skips outlines whose enclosed area is below the limit

questions.explanation: Filtering by area removes specks before measurement and labelling.

questions.prompt: With 5% specks and minimum area 50, the circle is labelled polygon. What changed?

options.text: Specks on its edge made the outline ragged, lowering circularity to 0.751
The circle moved off the image

questions.explanation: A longer, jagged perimeter lowers 4πA/P² below the 0.83 circle rule.

tutorials.title: 6. OpenCV histograms, equalization and Otsu thresholds
tutorials.summary: Read an intensity histogram, let Otsu choose a threshold, and see when equalization helps or hurts segmentation.

lessons.title: Histograms show where intensities sit
lessons.text: A histogram counts how many pixels have each intensity. The lab groups the 256 gray levels into 32 bins of 8 levels and reports spread, the standard deviation of intensity. The preset dims the lamp scene with brightness 0.7 and squeezes it toward mid-gray with contrast 0.4. Only three levels remain: 7835 background pixels at 85, 8032 board pixels at 92 and 517 lamp pixels at 144. Spread is 10.29. The lamp is still distinct, but a fixed threshold of 150 now selects nothing.

lessons.title: Otsu chooses a threshold from the histogram
lessons.text: Otsu's method tests every threshold and keeps the one with the largest between-class variance, so the two groups are as separate as possible. OpenCV returns that threshold, and THRESH_BINARY selects pixels above it. On the preset Otsu returns 92: background and board fall at or below it, the lamp above. The mask is the 517 lamp pixels, with IoU 1. The output panel shows the gray image after any equalization; the measurements describe the Otsu mask. Otsu always splits into two groups, so with three it must merge two of them.

lessons.title: Global equalization versus CLAHE
lessons.text: Global equalization remaps each level through the cumulative histogram to spread levels across 0–255. Here background becomes 0, board 240 and lamp 255; spread jumps from 10.29 to 120.37. Now the board sits next to the lamp, so Otsu returns 0 and selects both: 8549 pixels, IoU 0.060. The IoT preview still reports a detection, with bright_fraction 0.5218. CLAHE equalizes an 8 × 8 grid of tiles and clips each tile histogram first. At clip limit 2, spread only reaches 10.52, Otsu returns 97 and IoU stays 1. More contrast is not better segmentation.

formulas.title: Otsu's between-class variance
formulas.equation: σB²(T) = ω₀ ω₁ (μ₀ − μ₁)²
formulas.symbols: T: candidate threshold; ω₀, ω₁: fractions of pixels at or below T and above T; μ₀, μ₁: their mean intensities. Otsu returns the T with the largest σB².
formulas.example: Preset at T = 92: ω₀ ≈ 0.968, ω₁ ≈ 0.032, μ₀ ≈ 88.5 and μ₁ = 144, so σB² ≈ 94. At T = 85, σB² ≈ 26, so 92 wins.

formulas.title: Global histogram equalization
formulas.equation: v′ = round(255 × (cdf(v) − cdfmin) / (N − cdfmin))
formulas.symbols: v: input level; cdf(v): number of pixels at or below v; cdfmin: count at the darkest occupied level; N: total pixels; v′: output level. This is the mapping OpenCV equalizeHist uses.
formulas.example: Board level 92: cdf = 15867, cdfmin = 7835 and N = 16384, so v′ = round(255 × 8032 / 8549) = 240.

steps: Open the preset. Read the histogram, spread and Otsu threshold, and confirm 517 selected pixels with IoU 1.
Switch the pipeline to grayscale threshold at 150 and confirm that the lamp disappears. Then return to the histogram pipeline.
Set equalization to global. Compare the histogram and spread before and after, then explain why Otsu returns 0 and IoU falls to 0.060.
Set equalization to CLAHE with clip limit 2, then 4. Record each Otsu threshold and IoU, and compare bright_fraction with the global case.

practice.prompt: The preset has gray levels 85, 92 and 144. Why does a fixed threshold of 150 select nothing?

options.text: Every level is at or below 150
The lamp moved out of view

practice.explanation: THRESH_BINARY selects values above the threshold. The brightest level, the lamp, is 144.

practice.prompt: What does Otsu's method maximize?

options.text: The between-class variance of the two groups

practice.explanation: It picks the split that best separates the two group means, weighted by the group sizes.

questions.prompt: Otsu returns 92 and the lab applies THRESH_BINARY. Which pixels are selected?
questions.explanation: THRESH_BINARY keeps values strictly greater than the threshold.

questions.prompt: Global equalization raises spread from 10.29 to 120.37, but IoU falls to 0.060. Why?

options.text: It moves the board next to the lamp, so Otsu separates background from board plus lamp

questions.explanation: The levels become 0, 240 and 255. The best two-group split now lies between 0 and 240.

questions.prompt: How does CLAHE differ from global equalization?

options.text: It equalizes small tiles and clips histogram peaks to limit amplification
It converts the image to HSV
It applies a fixed threshold of 150

questions.explanation: The clip limit caps how far any tile can stretch; with clip limit 2, spread here only reaches 10.52.

questions.prompt: What does spread measure in this lab?

options.text: The standard deviation of pixel intensity

questions.explanation: Spread is the square root of the mean squared difference between each pixel and the mean intensity.

questions.prompt: When can Otsu choose a split that misses your target?

options.text: When the image has more than two intensity groups
Only when the image is square
Never; it always isolates the target

questions.explanation: Otsu models two classes. With three, it must merge two, as the global-equalization case shows.

tutorials.title: 7. OpenCV perspective correction with four corners
tutorials.summary: Find a tilted card's four corners, compute a homography and warp the card onto a flat, front-on frame.

lessons.title: Find and order four corners
lessons.text: A camera tilted toward a flat card makes the far edge look shorter. The lab thresholds the document scene at 150, traces external contours and keeps the largest outline whose polygon has exactly 4 corners. At tilt 0.4 those corners are top-left (42, 34), top-right (86, 34), bottom-right (98, 98) and bottom-left (30, 98). Order matters. The smallest x + y is top-left and the largest is bottom-right; the smallest y − x is top-right and the largest is bottom-left. Swapped corners would mirror or twist the output.

lessons.title: A homography maps the card onto the frame
lessons.text: For a flat surface and an ideal pinhole camera, a 3 × 3 homography maps card points to image points. It has 8 unknowns and each corner pair gives 2 equations, so getPerspectiveTransform solves it from 4 pairs. warpPerspective fills each output pixel by mapping it back into the source and interpolating. The lab sends the four detected corners to the corners of the 128 × 128 frame. The mapping divides by a scale that varies across the image: 16-pixel steps down the card's centre line become about 43, 34, 27 and 23 pixels.

lessons.title: Read the result and know its limits
lessons.text: The lab reports whether a card was found, its ordered corners and its contour area: 3531 px² at tilt 0.4. The mask fills the card outline, so IoU is 1. The card is gray level 235: from threshold 235 up nothing passes, and the lab reports no card instead of guessing. The generator fakes tilt by linear interpolation, not a camera model, so the warped printed square sits low and is wider at the top. Real lenses bend straight lines: calibrate and undistort first. The IoT preview only reports an event; nothing reads the card.

formulas.title: Homography between two planes
formulas.equation: s·[u, v, 1]ᵀ = H·[x, y, 1]ᵀ;  u = (h₁₁x + h₁₂y + h₁₃)/s,  v = (h₂₁x + h₂₂y + h₂₃)/s,  s = h₃₁x + h₃₂y + 1
formulas.symbols: (x, y): source pixel; (u, v): output pixel; H: 3 × 3 homography with h₃₃ = 1, which leaves 8 unknowns; s: projective scale. Four corner pairs give the 8 equations.
formulas.example: For the tilt-0.4 corners, s is about 1.41 along the card's top edge and 2.18 along its bottom edge, so the top is stretched more.

formulas.title: Ordering corners by sums and differences
formulas.equation: TL = min(x + y);  BR = max(x + y);  TR = min(y − x);  BL = max(y − x)
formulas.symbols: (x, y): corner coordinates in pixels, with y increasing downward. The rule assumes the card is not rotated close to 45°, where two corners tie.

steps: Open the preset. Record the four ordered corners, the card area and IoU, and compare the source with the rectified output.
Set tilt to 0, then 0.6. Record how the top corners move and how the card area changes.
Raise the threshold to 240 and confirm that the lab reports no card. Lower it until the card returns and note the highest working value.
Move the card with the offset slider and confirm that the corners follow. Then explain why the printed square is not centred after the warp.

practice.prompt: How many corner pairs does getPerspectiveTransform need?
practice.explanation: A homography has 8 unknowns, and each point pair gives 2 equations.

practice.prompt: Which corner has the smallest x + y?
practice.explanation: Image x grows rightward and y grows downward, so the top-left corner has the smallest sum.

questions.prompt: Corners (86, 34) and (30, 98) have y − x of −52 and 68. Which is top-right?

options.text: Neither; y − x cannot identify corners

questions.explanation: A top-right corner has large x and small y, so its y − x is the smallest.

questions.prompt: Why do equal 16-pixel steps down the tilted card not stay equal after the warp?

options.text: The homography divides by a scale that changes across the image

questions.explanation: The division makes the mapping non-linear, and the far edge is stretched most.

questions.prompt: At threshold 240 the lab finds no card. What should a deployed pipeline do?

options.text: Report no card and skip the warp
Guess corners at the image edges

questions.explanation: A missing measurement should be reported, not replaced with an invented one.

questions.prompt: What must come before a homography when a real lens bends straight lines?

options.text: Nothing; a homography removes all distortion

questions.explanation: A homography keeps straight lines straight, so it cannot model lens distortion.

questions.prompt: How does warpPerspective fill each output pixel?

options.text: It copies the nearest card corner
It maps the pixel back into the source and interpolates

questions.explanation: The lab uses linear interpolation between the four nearest source pixels.

tutorials.title: 8. OpenCV Hough transform: lane lines and round markers
tutorials.summary: Let edge pixels vote for straight lane edges and round lamps, then turn the segments into a robot steering preview.

lessons.title: Edge pixels vote for lines
lessons.text: The Hough transform describes a line by its distance ρ from the origin and the angle θ of its normal. Every edge pixel votes for all lines through it; lines with many votes win. The lab blurs the lanes scene with a 3 × 3 Gaussian, runs Canny, then calls HoughLinesP with 1-pixel ρ and 1° θ steps. The accumulator threshold sets the votes a line needs. Segments below the minimum length are dropped, and gaps up to the maximum gap are bridged. Results are segment end points, not infinite lines.

lessons.title: From lane segments to a steering preview
lessons.text: The preset finds 4 segments at about ±70°. Canny marks both edges of each painted lane, so each lane gives two segments. The reported angle is the segment direction, atan2(Δy, Δx), with y pointing down. The lab draws the segments 3 pixels wide into the mask, and the robot preview steers on that mask's centroid. Centred lanes give error 0.009. Offset 20 moves both lanes right: error 0.16, so angular.z = −0.16. Drawn lines are not a filled target, so IoU is not reported. At accumulator threshold 80, no line gets enough votes.

lessons.title: Circles, and what Hough cannot know
lessons.text: HoughCircles with HOUGH_GRADIENT runs its own Canny step with the lab's high edge threshold, then votes for centres along gradient directions. The accumulator threshold sets the votes a centre needs; radii outside the set range are ignored. On the IoT lamp, threshold 15 finds one circle at (63.5, 63.5) with radius 12.5, close to the drawn lamp of radius 13 around (64, 64). Threshold 25 finds none. Occlusion 0.4 hides the lamp's top, so the fit moves to (65.5, 65.5) with radius 10.6. Hough votes for any straight or round edge; it does not know what a lane or a lamp is.

formulas.title: A line in Hough space
formulas.equation: ρ = x cos θ + y sin θ
formulas.symbols: (x, y): edge pixel (px); θ: angle of the line's normal; ρ: signed distance from the image origin (px). Each edge pixel adds a vote to every (ρ, θ) cell it satisfies.
formulas.example: The first left-lane segment runs from (22, 127) to (54, 40). With θ ≈ 20.2°, both end points give ρ ≈ 64.5 px, so they vote for the same cell.

formulas.title: Segment angle and length
formulas.equation: angle = atan2(y₂ − y₁, x₂ − x₁);  length = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)
formulas.symbols: (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂): segment end points (px), with y increasing downward; angle in degrees. This is the segment direction that the lab reports, 90° away from the Hough θ.

steps: Open the preset. Read the four segments' end points, angles and lengths, and pair each segment with a painted lane.
Set the offset to 20. Record the normalized error and the angular.z request, and explain the sign.
Raise the accumulator threshold to 60, then 80, and count the segments each time. Return it to 30.
Switch to the IoT theme and circle detection with accumulator threshold 15. Record the circle, try threshold 25, then return to 15 and add occlusion 0.4.

practice.prompt: In ρ = x cos θ + y sin θ, what does one edge pixel do?

options.text: Votes for every line that passes through it
Becomes a line segment on its own

practice.explanation: Each (ρ, θ) cell collects votes, and cells where many pixels agree become lines.

practice.prompt: Why does each painted lane give two segments?

options.text: Canny marks both edges of the painted stripe

practice.explanation: A stripe has a left and a right boundary, and each one is a straight edge.

questions.prompt: Accumulator threshold 80 returns no segments on the lanes preset. Why?

options.text: No (ρ, θ) cell collects 80 votes from the edge pixels

questions.explanation: The accumulator threshold is a minimum vote count, and these lane edges never reach it.

questions.prompt: With offset 20 the normalized error is 0.16. Which yaw rate does the preview request?
questions.explanation: The robot adapter requests angular.z = −ex: a clockwise turn toward lanes on the right.

questions.prompt: What does HOUGH_GRADIENT use the lab's high edge threshold for?

options.text: The upper threshold of its internal Canny step
The number of circles to return

questions.explanation: OpenCV passes it as param1, the higher Canny threshold; the lower one is half of it.

questions.prompt: Occlusion 0.4 hides the top of the lamp. What happens to the detected circle?

options.text: The fit shifts to (65.5, 65.5) and shrinks to radius 10.6

questions.explanation: Only the visible edge votes, so a partial outline pulls the centre and the radius.

questions.prompt: Why is IoU not reported for Hough lines?

options.text: The mask holds 3-pixel drawn lines, not a filled target region

questions.explanation: An overlap score between thin drawn lines and filled lane paint would not be meaningful.

tutorials.title: 9. OpenCV template matching for a landing pad
tutorials.summary: Slide a pad template across the image, read the normalized correlation score, and test brightness, scale and occlusion.

lessons.title: Slide a template and score every position
lessons.text: Template matching compares a small reference image with every same-sized window of the scene. The lab cuts a 48 × 48 template from the centre of a clean drone-pad scene at scale 1, converts both to grayscale and calls matchTemplate. A 128 × 128 image gives 81 × 81 = 6561 windows. minMaxLoc returns the best score and that window's top-left corner: 1.0 at (40, 40) here. At or above the 0.6 threshold, the window gets a green outline and fills the mask. Below it, the outline is red and the mask stays empty.

lessons.title: Normalized correlation ignores brightness
lessons.text: TM_CCOEFF_NORMED subtracts the mean from the template and from each window, then divides by both standard deviations. A uniform brightness gain or offset cancels if no pixel clips, and the score stays between −1 and 1. Brightness 0.5 still scores 1. The score is not a probability: 0.6 is a threshold you choose from tests. The box covers 2304 pixels and the pad 1849, so IoU is 0.803 even for a perfect match. The drone preview uses the box centre: offset 25 moves the match to x = 65 and normalized_x to 0.394.

lessons.title: Scale, occlusion and absent targets
lessons.text: Plain template matching is not scale- or rotation-invariant. The template was cut at scale 1. Scale 0.8 still scores 0.631, but 0.7 scores 0.587 and 1.3 scores 0.416, below the threshold although the pad is visible. Occlusion 0.4 drops the score to 0.556. The IoT scene has no pad, yet minMaxLoc still returns a best window, with score 0.458; the threshold decides detection. A 3 × 3 blur on the scene alone lowers the score to 0.968, because the template is not blurred. Real systems search several scales or use feature-based methods.

formulas.title: Normalized correlation coefficient
formulas.equation: R(x,y) = Σ T′(i,j)·I′(x+i, y+j) / √(Σ T′(i,j)² · Σ I′(x+i, y+j)²)
formulas.symbols: T′: template minus its mean; I′: image window minus its mean; (x, y): window top-left corner (px); i, j: offsets inside the template; R: score from −1 to 1 (TM_CCOEFF_NORMED).
formulas.example: If every window pixel equals a × template + b with a > 0, the mean and the scale cancel and R = 1. Brightness 0.5 in the lab still gives 1.0.

formulas.title: Search positions and box overlap
formulas.equation: positions = (W − w + 1)(H − h + 1);  IoU = |box ∩ pad| / |box ∪ pad|
formulas.symbols: W, H: image size (px); w, h: template size (px); box: the 48 × 48 match rectangle; pad: the true target pixels.
formulas.example: (128 − 48 + 1)² = 6561 positions. A perfect match places the 1849-pixel pad inside the 2304-pixel box: IoU = 1849/2304 ≈ 0.803.

steps: Open the preset. Record the score, the match location and IoU, and explain why IoU is 0.803 for a perfect match.
Lower brightness to 0.5, then set the offset to 25. Record the score, the new location and the drone preview's normalized_x.
Reset brightness and offset. Set scale to 0.8, 0.7 and then 1.3, and record which scales still pass the 0.6 threshold.
Return scale to 1. Add occlusion 0.4, then switch to the IoT theme, and compare each best score with the threshold.

practice.prompt: How many window positions does a 48 × 48 template have in a 128 × 128 image?
Why does brightness 0.5 still score 1?

options.text: The template is re-cut from the dark scene
Mean subtraction and normalization cancel a uniform brightness gain

practice.explanation: TM_CCOEFF_NORMED compares patterns after removing each patch's mean and scale.

questions.prompt: The pad at scale 1.3 scores 0.416. What does that show?
questions.explanation: The same pad at another size no longer lines up with the fixed-size template.

questions.prompt: On the IoT scene, which has no pad, the lab still reports a best location. Why?

options.text: The lamp is a landing pad
minMaxLoc always returns a maximum; the threshold decides detection
Template matching cannot return low scores

questions.explanation: Every image has a best window among the 6561. Its score of 0.458 is below 0.6, so nothing is detected.

questions.prompt: Is a score of 0.9 a 90% probability that a pad is present?

options.text: No; it is a correlation score, and thresholds come from testing

questions.explanation: Correlation measures pattern similarity, not a calibrated probability.

questions.prompt: What does the reported match location mark?

options.text: The top-left corner of the best 48 × 48 window

questions.explanation: matchTemplate scores each window by its top-left corner; add 23.5 px to reach the window centre.

questions.prompt: Why is IoU 0.803 for a perfect match?

options.text: The match is in the wrong place
The 48 × 48 box (2304 px) is larger than the 1849-pixel pad

questions.explanation: IoU = 1849/2304 ≈ 0.803, because the box includes background around the pad.

tutorials.title: 10. Vision transformers: patches, tokens and attention
tutorials.summary: Explore the mathematics behind ViT by changing patch size, query location and attention temperature.

lessons.title: Turn an image into a token sequence
lessons.text: A vision transformer divides an image into patches, maps each flattened patch to an embedding and adds position information. Those tokens pass through transformer blocks. A trained model can then support classification or other vision tasks through a suitable head. This sandbox uses mean patch RGB plus coordinates as a five-value teaching embedding. It is intentionally much smaller than a ViT and has no trained patch projection, classifier, class token or prediction labels.

lessons.title: Queries compare with keys and mix values
lessons.text: For one selected query patch, compute dot products with all key vectors, divide by the square root of their dimension and apply softmax to obtain nonnegative weights summing to one. The weighted average of value vectors is the context. Here Q and K use the identity projection and V is mean RGB. Temperature changes the concentration of weights. Clicking a different patch changes the query; bright heatmap cells show where this head mixes information, not where an object was detected.

lessons.title: Distinguish model architecture from learned ability
lessons.text: A useful vision model learns weights from data and must be evaluated on images representative of deployment. A full transformer also contains normalization, residual connections, feed-forward layers and usually multiple heads and blocks. This explorer computes one attention row with fixed features; it cannot classify a drone pad or a robot obstacle. Use it to understand token cost and attention mathematics. Device actions require a validated perception output, so the integration bench rejects attention-only output.

formulas.title: Patch tokens and attention pairs
formulas.equation: N = (H/P)(W/P);  pairs = N²
formulas.symbols: H, W: image dimensions (pixels); P: square patch width (pixels); N: token count, excluding any class token. Assumes dimensions divide evenly.
formulas.example: A 128 × 128 image with P = 16 has 64 tokens and 4096 pairs. P = 8 gives 256 tokens and 65536 pairs: 16 times as many pairs.

formulas.title: Scaled dot-product attention
formulas.equation: A = softmax(QKᵀ / √dk);  Z = AV
formulas.symbols: Q, K: query/key matrices; V: value matrix; dk: key dimension; A: row-normalized attention weights; Z: weighted context. Explorer temperature additionally divides the logits.
formulas.example: Two equal logits give weights [0.5, 0.5]. With scalar values [0.2, 0.8], the context is 0.5.

steps: Choose a patch on the pad, then a background patch. Compare weights and context RGB.
Change patch size from 16 to 8 and compare token count and the full-matrix pair count.
Lower attention temperature and inspect whether weights become more concentrated.
Set position feature weight to zero and explain which spatial information this teaching embedding loses. Verify that attention mode cannot command connected devices.

practice.prompt: A 128 × 128 image with 16 × 16 patches has how many tokens before a class token?
practice.explanation: There are 8 patches across and 8 down: 8 × 8 = 64.

practice.prompt: What must each softmax weight row sum to?
practice.explanation: Softmax divides positive exponentials by their sum.

questions.prompt: Halving patch width from 16 to 8 changes the full attention pair count by…
questions.explanation: Token count quadruples, and its square grows by a factor of 16.

questions.prompt: What does a bright cell in this attention heatmap mean?

options.text: A larger mixing weight for the selected query
A calibrated probability of safe landing

questions.explanation: Attention weights describe information mixing, not detection confidence.

questions.prompt: Does this fixed attention explorer perform trained ViT classification?

options.text: Yes; it contains a pretrained classifier
Only when the patch size is 8
No; it demonstrates part of the computation

questions.explanation: The explorer has fixed features and no trained head or model weights.

questions.prompt: Equal logits over values 0.2 and 0.8 produce context…
questions.explanation: Equal logits yield equal weights: 0.5×0.2 + 0.5×0.8 = 0.5.

questions.prompt: Why include position information in image tokens?

options.text: To distinguish where image content appears
To convert pixels into motor voltage

questions.explanation: Without position information, the token features alone do not encode their spatial arrangement.

tutorials.title: 11. Integrating OpenCV and trained vision models
tutorials.summary: Design a perception interface, evaluate a pipeline and connect it to IoT, drone and robot software.

lessons.title: Give perception one explicit output contract
lessons.text: An integration pipeline separates acquisition, preprocessing, inference or image rules, validation and device adapters. OpenCV can prepare images and compute masks; a trained transformer can supply a different detector or classifier when its task and weights are appropriate. Both should produce a documented observation rather than directly controlling motors. Our teaching contract contains detected, normalized_x and area_fraction. The capstone routes this single observation to HTTP, serial and a ROS-style Twist interface.

lessons.title: Measure errors on representative examples
lessons.text: Evaluate images that vary in brightness, clutter, target position and occlusion. The sandbox knows the synthetic target mask and can report intersection-over-union for filled masks. Canny outlines are not compared to a filled target, so their IoU is marked not applicable. A high score on one generated image does not establish real-world performance. A trained model needs held-out evaluation and task-appropriate metrics; its confidence threshold must be chosen from evidence rather than from an attention heatmap.

lessons.title: Keep units, freshness and failure behavior explicit
lessons.text: A deployed adapter should check message shape, units, coordinate frame and age before accepting a measurement. Run heavy vision on a suitable companion processor and send compact observations to a controller. Include acquisition and inference time in the latency budget. The examples use a saved image and explicit local test endpoints; they do not install a camera, ROS or MQTT broker in the browser. The browser integration uses fresh button-triggered observations and the robot driver has a one-second command timeout.

formulas.title: Segmentation overlap
formulas.equation: IoU = |prediction ∩ target| / |prediction ∪ target|
formulas.symbols: IoU: dimensionless intersection-over-union. Compare compatible masks; this sandbox evaluates filled target masks only.
formulas.example: An intersection of 80 pixels and union of 100 pixels gives IoU = 0.8.

formulas.title: End-to-end latency and travel
formulas.equation: L = tacquire + tprocess + ttransport + tactuate;  d = vL
formulas.symbols: L: total latency (s); each t: stage duration (s); v: speed (m/s); d: travel during latency (m), ignoring acceleration.
formulas.example: 20 ms acquisition + 40 ms processing + 10 ms transport + 10 ms actuation = 80 ms. At 0.5 m/s, travel is 0.04 m.

steps: Record the default IoT threshold IoU. Increase occlusion and compare the score.
Lower the threshold enough to select background. Explain why a large selected area is not necessarily a good detection.
Inspect the JSON observation and each adapter payload in the integration bench. Trace units and signs.
Read the companion examples. Identify where a trained model could replace the mask producer while preserving downstream adapter contracts.

practice.prompt: Intersection 80 and union 100 give which IoU?
practice.explanation: Divide intersection size by union size.

practice.prompt: Four stages taking 20, 40, 10 and 10 ms total…
practice.explanation: Add all serial stage durations in the latency path.

questions.prompt: Where can a trained transformer fit into the integration pipeline?

options.text: As an automatic replacement for every controller
As a perception stage producing a validated observation
As an unexplained direct battery connection

questions.explanation: Keep task-specific perception separate from transport and actuation.

questions.prompt: Why is Canny IoU not shown against the filled target here?

options.text: Edge pixels and filled regions are different representations

questions.explanation: An outline should be evaluated against a compatible boundary target or boundary metric.

questions.prompt: At 0.5 m/s during 80 ms latency, the robot travels…
questions.explanation: Convert 80 ms to 0.08 s, then multiply by 0.5 m/s.

questions.prompt: Which data split should measure a trained model beyond its fitting examples?
questions.explanation: Independent examples help reveal generalization errors.

questions.prompt: What should a receiver verify before acting on perception?

options.text: Only that JSON contains a number

questions.explanation: A syntactically valid number can still use the wrong unit, frame or timestamp.

tutorials.title: 12. Capstone: connect vision, IoT, drones and robotics
tutorials.summary: Run one vision observation through three working simulated device adapters, then inspect failure cases.

lessons.title: One measurement, different device responsibilities
lessons.text: Start with the green drone-pad scene and an HSV mask. The perception stage computes selected area and horizontal centroid. A valid mask creates detected = true; an empty or tiny mask creates detected = false. Every click of Send observation captures the current result and routes it to three different devices. This teaches separation of responsibilities: the IoT endpoint represents an event, the drone bench exposes a pulse adapter, and the robot interprets a velocity message.

lessons.title: Follow the complete path to observable behavior
lessons.text: Start connected devices and wait for the 1.2-second low ESC signal. Sending a detected observation calls GET /on on the actual virtual ESP32 WebServer, transmits L, C or R to the actual clamped drone firmware, and publishes a Twist into the differential-drive model. The panels show the HTTP response, measured ESC pulse and motor RPM, and the robot pose after one second. Inspect these outputs instead of assuming that constructing a JSON payload completed the integration.

lessons.title: Test no target and separate learning models
lessons.text: Move the pad left and right, then exclude green with the hue controls. No target maps to HTTP /off, serial X with disarm, and zero robot velocity. Attention-only mode supplies no observation and disables sending; fixed attention weights are not detector output. The three demonstrations share a perception contract but do not form a physical autonomous team. The ESC is props-off, the camera scenes are generated, and the robot world does not provide a camera. These boundaries make each observed response interpretable.

formulas.title: Bounded adapter outputs
formulas.equation: ωrobot = −ex rad/s;  pulse = 1150 (left), 1200 (center), 1250 (right) µs
formulas.symbols: ex: normalized image error; left: ex < −0.1; right: ex > 0.1; otherwise center. No target gives 1000 µs and disarm. These ESC values are teaching signals, not a flight mix.
formulas.example: For ex = +0.3, the robot requests −0.3 rad/s and the props-off ESC receives serial R, requesting 1250 µs.

formulas.title: Verify response with a measured delta
formulas.equation: Δpose = poseafter − posebefore;  expected straight Δx = vΔt
formulas.symbols: Pose: x/y position (m) and yaw (rad); v: forward speed (m/s); Δt: virtual interval (s). The straight case assumes yaw zero and no obstacle.
formulas.example: A centered observation requests 0.15 m/s. Over one second at yaw zero, expected forward travel is 0.15 m.

steps: Start connected devices. Keep HSV hue 40–90 and send the initial centered pad observation. Verify HTTP 200, ESC 1200 µs and changed robot pose.
Move the pad right by 25 px, send again and verify serial R, ESC 1250 µs and negative robot yaw correction.
Exclude green by setting hue minimum and maximum to 0, then send the no-target result. Verify LED off, ESC 1000 µs and no additional robot motion.
Switch to attention mode. Explain why sending is disabled, then export measurements and settings to document the experiment.

practice.prompt: Which observation field is shared by all three adapters?
practice.explanation: Each device can interpret the same detected/no-target observation in its own way.

practice.prompt: What verifies the virtual IoT command actually reached the server?

options.text: Only the color of a course card
The HTTP response returned by the simulated WebServer

practice.explanation: The returned status and body provide application-level evidence of handling.

questions.prompt: For ex = +0.3, which drone serial code does this adapter send?
questions.explanation: Positive error above 0.1 maps to the right-hand teaching signal R.

questions.prompt: What happens on a no-target observation?

options.text: LED off, ESC low/disarmed and robot stop
The previous action is repeated forever

questions.explanation: Each adapter has an explicit no-target mapping.

questions.prompt: Why does attention-only mode disable Send observation?

options.text: Its weights are not a validated detection result

questions.explanation: This fixed attention explorer supplies no detector observation.

questions.prompt: At 0.15 m/s for 1 s with zero yaw, expected travel is…
questions.explanation: Distance is speed times time.

questions.prompt: Does this capstone implement autonomous drone landing?

options.text: No; the drone demonstration is a clamped props-off signal adapter
Yes; color alone proves a safe landing site
Only if the HTTP status is 200

questions.explanation: A landing controller requires additional state estimation, calibration and flight control beyond this signal demonstration.
